volumes.title: A Wet Monday in October
volumes.text:
I came to Quill’s Bindery in Needle Lane on a wet Monday in October, with my indentures in one pocket and a herring pie from my mother in the other. I am Robin Ellery, fourteen, from Saltby on the Grey Coast, where my family mends nets. Mrs Quill looked at my hands before she looked at my face. “Knots,” she said. “Good. Wipe your feet.”

The shop smelled of paste and leather and warm cat. The cat is called Kettle, after a stitch, and she sleeps in the paper drawer. I was given a broom, a stool, and three rules: never touch the gold, never hurry the press, never put a cup on the bench.

High on a shelf stood one small brown book, so crooked that it leaned on nothing. I asked whose it was. “Mine,” said Mrs Quill. “My first. Sweep.”

volumes.title: Folding With the Bone
volumes.text:
My first real work at Quill’s Bindery was folding. A book begins as large flat sheets, and each must be folded in half, and in half again, until it is a little bundle of pages called a section. Mrs Quill gave me two hundred sheets and a bone folder, a smooth blade of bone for pressing a crease down sharp.

Paper, I learned, has a grain, like wood. Fold with it and the sheet lies down quietly. Fold against it and it fights, and the crease comes out cracked and sulky. By noon I could find the grain with my eyes shut, by bending the sheet and feeling which way it gave.

By evening I had a blister, a hundred and ninety good sections, and ten that Mrs Quill held up to the window one by one without a word. Kettle the cat slept on those.

volumes.title: The Kettle Stitch
volumes.text:
In my second month as apprentice to Mrs Quill, the binder in Needle Lane, I was let near the sewing frame. It is a wooden gallows the width of the bench, with cords strung up it like a harp. The folded sections are sewn to those cords until they are a book.

Here, at last, I knew something. I grew up in Saltby mending herring nets, and a needle is a needle. The stitch that locks each section to the one below is called the kettle stitch, and it is very nearly a net-mender’s hitch done sideways. My fingers found it before my head did.

Mrs Quill watched me sew eight sections. She pulled at the thread with one fingernail. It did not give. “Hm,” she said, and went back to her own bench. I have since learned that “Hm” is the top of her scale.

volumes.title: Paste Has Opinions
volumes.text:
Midwinter at Quill’s Bindery, and I, Robin Ellery, apprentice, was promoted to paste. Paste is flour and water cooked in a pan until it turns from milk to something like cold porridge. It sounds like nothing. It has opinions. Look away for the length of a sneeze and it goes to lumps, and Mrs Quill can find a lump in the dark.

My first panful would have mended a boat. My second ran off the brush like soup. My third was good, and I was so pleased that I carried it across the shop to show her, tripped over Kettle the cat, and pasted the cat, the floor, and a customer’s umbrella.

Kettle forgave nobody for two days. Mrs Quill said only that paste comes off everything with warm water, which is the whole point of paste, and that I might now prove it.

volumes.title: The Night Press
volumes.text:
There is a great iron press in the corner of Mrs Quill’s bindery in Needle Lane, with a wheel on top like a ship’s. When a book has been pasted it goes between boards under that wheel and stays the night. That was the second rule I was given as her apprentice: never hurry the press.

In January I hurried the press. I had made my first whole book, a plain account book for the chandler, and I could not wait until morning to see it. I let it out after supper, by candle. It looked perfect. By breakfast the boards had curled outward like the wings of a startled hen.

Mrs Quill turned it over in her hands. She did not scold. She damped it, set it back under the wheel, and made me wind it down myself. “Two nights now,” she said. “It charges interest.”

volumes.title: Rounding and Backing
volumes.text:
The spine of a book is not flat. I had never noticed until Mrs Quill, the binder I am apprenticed to, handed me a hammer. The sewn book is clamped with its back upward and tapped, gently, from the middle outward, until the back swells into a curve and the pages shoulder over to grip the boards. It is called rounding and backing. It is mostly a matter of not hitting your thumb.

I hit my thumb. I also finished, in February, the first book that was mine from fold to cloth: a small blank notebook in green. It leans. Stood on the bench, it bows a little to the left, like a polite man in a wind.

I expected the stove. Instead Mrs Quill reached up and stood it on the high shelf, beside her own crooked brown first book from forty years ago. They lean toward each other.

volumes.title: The Paring Knife
volumes.text:
Spring came to Needle Lane, and with it leather. Mrs Quill laid a skin of brown goat on the stone and showed me how its edges must be shaved thin as a leaf, so that the leather turns neatly over the boards. This is paring. The knife is kept sharper than anything else in the shop, Mrs Quill included.

A skin costs more than I earn in a quarter. I knew that. I held my breath, leaned in, and pared a hole clean through it the size of a sixpence.

I, Robin Ellery, apprentice, confessed at once, because there is no hiding a hole from a binder. Mrs Quill looked through it at me with one eye. Then she cut the piece free, wrote my name and the date on the back, and put it in the patch drawer. “Everyone’s is in there,” she said. “Mine is bigger.”

volumes.title: Gold on the Breath
volumes.text:
I had been seven months at Quill’s Bindery before I was allowed to touch the gold. It comes in leaves beaten so thin that they have no weight at all. You lift one on the flat of a knife. If you breathe out, it leaves, and you find it later on the cat.

The letters are brass, each on its own handle, warmed on the stove and pressed through the gold into the leather. Mrs Quill gave me the spine of a town almanac to letter. I held my breath for the whole of EMBERWICK, and every letter sat straight and bright. Then I breathed, and looked. I had picked up the M upside down. The spine read EWBERWICK.

“Well,” said Mrs Quill, “now you have done it once.” She showed me how gold is coaxed off again, which takes an afternoon. Kettle the cat stayed gilded for a week.

volumes.title: Alone at the Counter
volumes.text:
In June Mrs Quill went down to the Lowlands for a day to quarrel with the paper mill, and left me, Robin Ellery, eight months an apprentice, in charge of the bindery in Needle Lane. “Take in work. Promise nothing by Friday,” she said.

Three people came. A boy asked whether we could mend a kite. A lady left a songbook that had lost its back. And old Farmer Dunnock put down a stock book so tired that it sighed, and asked the price of mending it. I looked at the sewing. I said ninepence. It was a two-shilling job. I knew it as the door closed. I spent the afternoon rehearsing my confession to the cat.

Mrs Quill heard me out. “Then ninepence it is,” she said. “A binder’s word is part of the binding. You may pay the difference in sweeping.” I am still sweeping.

volumes.title: The Proof Book Set
volumes.text:
On the last Monday of September Mrs Quill cleared the small bench by the window and laid out cream paper, two boards, thread and half a skin of blue goat. “Your proof book,” she said.

Every apprentice makes one at the end of the first year. I am to bind a blank book alone, from the first fold to the last gold letter, in seven days. She will not help. She will not look. She has turned her own stool to face the wall, which I think is harder for her than for me.

If it passes, my indentures are signed for six years more and I stay in Needle Lane. If not, I go home to Saltby and the nets. She did not say that part. She only moved the paring knife an inch nearer my hand, and told Kettle the cat to keep off the paper.

volumes.title: Seven Days Alone
volumes.text:
This was the week of my proof book: one blank book bound alone, with Mrs Quill’s back turned, to show what a year at her bench has taught me. I folded on Monday, feeling for the grain. I sewed on Tuesday with the net-mender’s hitch my fingers knew before I came. On Wednesday I rounded the back and spared both thumbs. On Thursday I pared the blue leather, and it held.

On Friday I pasted the endpapers, and the back one slid. It sits a hair’s breadth askew, and by the time I saw it the paste had taken.

I could have hidden it. A pressed flower would cover the place. I thought about that for a whole cup of tea. Then I put the book under the great press for two full nights, untouched, and on Sunday I lettered the spine with every letter the right way up.

volumes.title: Signed Where Nobody Looks
volumes.text:
A year to the week after I came to Needle Lane, Mrs Quill turned her stool round and took up my proof book. She pulled at the sewing with a fingernail. She found the crooked back endpaper in four seconds, and I said I had left it honest. “Hm,” she said. Then, which has never happened before: “The sewing is better than mine.”

She signed my indentures for six more years. Then she gave me a bone folder gone yellow and thin at the tip. It was old Mr Tane’s, who taught her at this same bench, and she has folded with it for forty years.

Binders sign where nobody looks. I tooled R.E. inside the back board. The pages were blank, so I have filled them with this account. My leaning green notebook stays on the high shelf. Kettle the cat sleeps on the indentures.

volumes.title: To Whoever Comes After
volumes.text:
I am Josiah Tane, binder, of Needle Lane in Emberwick, and I have stood at this bench forty-one years. My knuckles have begun to object. I have no apprentice, so I am writing down what I know for whoever takes the bench after me. That is you. Sit up.

The trade has three parts and I have put them on the cover: paper, paste, and patience. You may buy the first and cook the second. The third you will have to grow yourself, slowly, like a quince.

I begin because of what came in this morning. The spring flood got into the Town Hall cellar, and the clerk has brought me the Flood Book in a roasting tin. It is the town’s record of every high water on the Ember for a hundred and sixty years, and it is, at present, soup. We shall mend it together as we go.

volumes.title: Paper Has a Grain
volumes.text:
First lesson, from Josiah Tane’s bench in Needle Lane to whoever stands here next. Paper has a grain. The fibres lie mostly one way, as the hairs do on a cat. Bend a sheet both ways and you will feel it yield in one and stiffen in the other. Fold with the grain, always. A book folded against it will never lie open, and will spend its life trying to shut on the reader’s thumb.

There. That is a third of what I know.

As to the Flood Book, the town’s drowned river record: I have taken it apart. It came to two hundred and twelve leaves. Each is drying between blotters pegged on strings across the shop, and I go about my own bindery ducking like a man in a laundry. Never light a fire to hurry wet paper. Open a window and go for a walk.

volumes.title: Paper Remembers Water
volumes.text:
You, at my bench: know that paper never forgets a wetting. It dries, but it dries wavy, with a brown tide line to show how far the water came. We call the waviness cockling. You cannot scold it out. You can only damp the leaf again and let it dry flat under a weighted board, and wait.

I, Josiah Tane, have two hundred and twelve such leaves this month. They are the Flood Book of Emberwick, which was caught in the spring flood it existed to record. I find that funnier than the town clerk does.

Each leaf carries a year, and a height taken at the third arch of the bridge, in the hand of whoever was clerk. Some wrote small. One drew a little wave. I have read every page while pressing it. Nobody has read the whole book in a century, and I recommend the job.

volumes.title: Mending a Tear
volumes.text:
A torn page is mended with a strip of thin tissue and a little paste. Here is the secret, and I, Josiah Tane, had to be told it too: tear the tissue, never cut it. A cut edge is a wall. A torn edge is feathered, with a thousand small fibres that hold to the page like burrs to a stocking. Done well, the mend vanishes when the leaf lies flat.

The Flood Book of Emberwick, which I am rebuilding this year, has thirty-four tears. The worst runs clean through the entry for the Great Flood, parting the feet from the inches. I have put the number back together.

A small face has taken to watching through my window from Needle Lane. It belongs to the chandler’s girl. When I look up, it goes. When I mend, it returns. I have started holding the work where it can see.

volumes.title: Paste Is Only Flour
volumes.text:
Now paste. The young expect a secret, so I, Josiah Tane, binder, will disappoint you at once: paste is flour and water, cooked and stirred until smooth, then strained through muslin. A good cook could make it. A good cook should not, because she will want to add salt.

Make it fresh. In summer it turns within three days, and you will know by the smell, and so will the customer.

Here is why we use so humble a thing when the joiner next door has strong glue. Whatever paste does, clean water gently undoes. Some binder a hundred years on will need to take your book apart, as I am taking apart the town’s Flood Book this year. Paste lets go for him without a fight. That is manners. You are not the last person who will love this book, so do not bind as if you were.

volumes.title: Thin Coats, Twice
volumes.text:
Whoever you are at this bench after me, you will use too much paste. Everybody does. It feels generous. Then the paper drinks it, swells, wrinkles, and squeezes the extra out at the edges, where it finds your sleeve.

The rule that I, Josiah Tane, was taught with a ruler, and now offer you free: a thin coat, from the middle outward, like spokes from a hub. Let it sink in. Then another thin coat. Two thin coats hold better than one thick, and that is true of paste, paint, and apologies.

This week I pasted a narrow strip of new paper down the fold of every leaf of the Flood Book, the river record I am rebuilding, so that there is something sound to sew through. The chandler’s girl was at the window. I wiped my brush with a flourish. I am not too old to show off.

volumes.title: What the Spine Was Hiding
volumes.text:
Binders waste nothing. When you take down an old book, you, my successor, must look inside the spine, because the binder before you will have lined it with whatever scrap lay nearest.

I soaked the old lining off the Flood Book of Emberwick this week. It came away in warm water, as paste always will, and floated up in three strips. One was a baker’s bill for forty loaves. One was half a ballad about a goose. The third was in ink: R. Mott bound this, the wet year, with a cold in his head.

I never heard of R. Mott. He stood at a bench in this town a hundred and sixty years before me, sneezing. I, Josiah Tane, have dried his note and shall put it back, with a strip of my own beneath it. I have not yet decided what to complain of.

volumes.title: Thread, and Not Pulling
volumes.text:
Sewing is where a book becomes one thing instead of many. The folded sections go to the sewing frame, and the thread runs through each fold and round the cords. Now the lesson, successor: do not pull. Draw the thread snug and stop. A book sewn tight as a drum will crack along its joints within the year. It needs a little slack to breathe in, as a marriage does, or a boot.

I, Josiah Tane, sewed the Flood Book of Emberwick this week on five cords, with forty blank leaves added at the end for floods to come.

It rained on Thursday, and the chandler’s girl came in to drip by my stove. Her name is Hesper. She is nine. She watched me sew for an hour and asked only one question, which was why I did not pull it tight. I nearly dropped the needle.

volumes.title: The Press Does the Work
volumes.text:
We come to patience, the third part of the trade, which cannot be bought. I, Josiah Tane, will start you on it with the press.

When a book is pasted and put between boards under the iron wheel, your work stops and the press’s begins. You will want to look. You will think of reasons. Do not. A book let out early curls its boards in the night to spite you. Wind it down, bank the stove, and go home. Nothing a binder does after dark is as useful to the book as his sleeping.

The Flood Book, our town’s river record, went under the wheel on Monday, and I left it there until Thursday. I spent the days between teaching Hesper, the chandler’s girl, to sweep paper shavings toward the bin and not merely around it. She is paid a penny a week and a look at the gold.

volumes.title: Leather Will Not Be Hurried
volumes.text:
Leather is skin, and has not forgotten it. Damp it and it stretches kindly round a book. Rush it and it sulks, shrinks as it dries, and drags the boards awry. So, you at my bench: pare your edges thin, paste the skin, and then let it rest a few minutes before you lift it. Use that time to wash your hands. Leather shows every thumb.

I, Josiah Tane, covered the Flood Book of Emberwick this week in brown calf, river colour, which seemed only civil. Drawing it over the five cords took a whole morning and all the language I had.

Then it must dry slowly, away from the stove, for days. Hesper, the chandler’s child who sweeps for me, asked each morning if it was ready. On the fourth day she stopped asking and simply went and looked at it. That is the beginning of a binder.

volumes.title: Lettering in Gold
volumes.text:
Gold leaf is the last thing put on a book and the first thing anybody sees, which is unfair to the sewing. The leaf is laid on the leather; a warm brass letter is pressed through it; the gold stays where the heat touched, and the rest brushes away. Breathe out at the wrong moment and you have gilded your eyebrows.

Forty-one years I, Josiah Tane, have done this, and this autumn my hands shake. So I lettered the Flood Book of Emberwick one letter a day. FLOOD took a week, and BOOK most of another. I rested the hand and came back. Nobody told me slowness could be used as a tool, like a knife. I am telling you.

The second O sits a whisker low. Hesper, the chandler’s girl, spotted it from the door. I have left it. A book made by hand should admit to the hand.

volumes.title: Home to the Town Hall
volumes.text:
On the last day of October I, Josiah Tane, carried the Flood Book back to the Town Hall. It left in a roasting tin in spring. It returns with two hundred and twelve mended leaves, forty new ones, and a note in the spine: J. Tane rebound this, the year his hands gave notice. He was helped.

The clerk had kept this year’s flood height on a slip in his waistcoat. He wrote it on the first clean page, and we both stood looking at it rather longer than a number deserves.

So that book is done, and so is this one. I shall leave it in the bench drawer. Hesper, the chandler’s girl, asked this morning why paper bends easier one way than the other. I have sent her to wash her hands. You, whoever you are, may begin again at the second chapter; she is about to.

volumes.title: A Trough on a Handcart
volumes.text:
Ilse Farrow came into Emberwick in April behind a handcart. On the cart rode a shallow wooden trough, a bundle of combs, eleven stoppered jars, and a hatbox with no hat in it. She was a marbler. She made the swirled papers that binders paste inside the covers of good books, and she rented the old wash-house on Ropewalk, by the river, because marbling wants water and a stone floor.

In the hatbox was one small book. It had been her grandmother Marta’s, and Marta had marbled its endpapers in this town, fifty years before. They were slate blue and rust and a thread of yellow, and every vein in them ran double, as if the pattern had shivered while it was being made.

Ilse had tried for nine years to make that paper. Marta had left no word of how. So Ilse had come to ask the town.

volumes.title: Stone Pattern, Plain
volumes.text:
A marbler floats her colours on a trough of thickened water, called size, and lays a sheet of paper on them. The paper lifts the picture off whole. Nothing is left behind, so no two sheets are ever alike.

Ilse Farrow began her first week in the Emberwick wash-house with the oldest pattern there is. She shook drops of colour from a brush of broom straw and let them spread into rings, until the trough looked like the bed of a stream. Stone pattern. She made forty sheets, and the binder in Needle Lane bought them all for ledgers.

In the evening she mixed blue, rust and yellow, and tried for her grandmother’s lost paper, the one whose veins ran double. The colours sat on the size as bright and hard as boiled sweets. She hung the sheet up to dry anyway. It would do for somebody’s ledger.

volumes.title: The Herring Comb
volumes.text:
In May the harbour-master at Saltby, down on the Grey Coast, sent to Emberwick for endpapers for his new log. Ilse Farrow, the marbler lately come to the wash-house on Ropewalk, made him a combed pattern. She laid her colours in stripes across the trough and pulled a wide-toothed comb from end to end. The stripes bent into rows of small arches, each tucked under the last, like scales. She called it Herring Comb. The harbour-master ordered twenty more.

Afterwards she took her grandmother Marta’s little book from its hatbox and held the old endpapers beside the new. Marta’s pattern had been combed too; she could see the arches. But across them ran that fine doubling, every line with a faint twin beside it.

No comb did that. Ilse owned eleven combs and had made four more to be sure. She began to think the secret was not a tool.

volumes.title: Colours From the Dyer
volumes.text:
Next door to the wash-house where Ilse Farrow marbled her papers lived Emberwick’s dyer, Mr Osric Madder, whose hands were three colours on any day. He came round in June to complain of her drain, and stayed to look at the trough.

Ilse showed him what had brought her to town: her grandmother’s endpapers, blue, rust and yellow. Her own colours came out too loud beside them.

Mr Madder put on his spectacles and sniffed the page, which is how dyers read. The blue was woad, he said, any fool had that. The yellow was weld. But the rust was no dye at all. It was red earth, the sort that stains the sheep on the east side of the Northern Fells. “Yours is out of a jar. Hers was dug.” He drew her a map on the back of a bill. He never mentioned the drain again.

volumes.title: Fell Earth, Ground Fine
volumes.text:
It is a day’s walk from Emberwick to the east side of the Northern Fells, and Ilse Farrow, the marbler, made it in June with a trowel and two flour bags. She was after red earth for a colour. She found it in a cutting above a beck, where the sheep were faintly pink.

Back in her wash-house she ground the earth on a slab for three evenings, until it was finer than flour. Floated on the trough, it gave a rust so soft that she laughed aloud. That was the rust in her grandmother Marta’s endpapers, which Ilse had spent nine years trying to match.

She combed a sheet in blue, rust and yellow. The colours were right. But they lay crisp and still, and Marta’s had seemed to tremble. Ilse named the new pattern Fell Stone and sold it to a shepherd for his tally book.

volumes.title: What the Water Does
volumes.text:
By midsummer Ilse Farrow had her grandmother’s three colours and still not her grandmother’s paper. The old endpapers in the hatbox were soft at every edge, colour melting into colour. Hers, marbled in the Emberwick wash-house, came out sharp as cut tin.

It was Mr Madder the dyer who said it, leaning in her doorway eating a plum. “What water are you using?” The pump in the yard, she told him. His own dyes, he said, took one way with pump water and another with water from the Ember, and differently again in autumn, when rain brings the marsh peat down and the river runs brown as tea. Old Marta would never have carried pump water with a river at her door.

Ilse filled a bucket from the Ember. The colours spread more gently. Only a little; the summer river ran clear. She would have to wait for October.

volumes.title: The Waiting Patterns
volumes.text:
All that summer Ilse Farrow waited for the river to turn brown, and while she waited she worked. The wash-house door on Ropewalk stood open, and the children of Emberwick stood in it.

She made Gull’s Wing for the schoolmaster, grey feathers drawn out with a single pin. She made Marsh Light, green drops with a yellow heart, for a lady’s album. A boy called Tam, who had watched for a fortnight without blinking, was at last allowed to lay a sheet himself. He lifted it and stood holding his own wet paper as though it might fly off.

“Can you make that one again?” he asked. She could not, she told him, and neither could anybody. That was the trade. Which made it all the stranger, she thought that night, to have spent nine years trying to make her grandmother’s sheet a second time.

volumes.title: An Old Woman Remembers
volumes.text:
Mrs Hartle was ninety-one and had been a laundress, and in August she came down Ropewalk on two sticks to see who had taken her old wash-house. She found Ilse Farrow at the marbling trough, and sat down uninvited on the copper.

She remembered Marta. Marta Farrow had marbled in that very corner fifty years back, and had cursed the stone barges. They came down the Ember from the quarry then, and when one went by the whole floor hummed, and the water in every tub shook, and Marta’s colours with it. “Then one day she stopped cursing,” Mrs Hartle said, “and took to listening for them. She would stand with the paper in her hands, waiting.”

Ilse looked at her trough. Then she asked when the next barge was due, and Mrs Hartle laughed until she had to be given water. The quarry had closed twenty years ago.

volumes.title: Brown Water in October
volumes.text:
The rain came in the first week of October, and the Ember turned the colour of strong tea. Ilse Farrow, the marbler, carried eight buckets of it up to her wash-house on Ropewalk and made her size with river water, as her grandmother Marta must have done.

She floated the blue, the yellow and the red earth she had dug in the Fells. They opened on the brown water slowly, like sleepers stretching, and their edges ran soft into one another. When she lifted the sheet, she had to sit down. It was nearly her grandmother’s lost paper. It was a cousin of it.

But Marta’s veins ran double, every one, and Ilse’s ran single. She knew why now. The stone barges that once shook this floor were gone. She lacked only something very heavy going by outside, and that cannot be dug out of a hill.

volumes.title: Something Heavy Going By
volumes.text:
For a fortnight in October the wash-house on Ropewalk was the noisiest building in Emberwick. Ilse Farrow, the marbler, needed her trough to tremble as it had trembled for her grandmother when the stone barges passed, and there were no barges any more.

She stamped. The colours jumped and tore. Mr Madder the dyer lent his two apprentices to leap off the copper, which made rings like a dropped stone. A boy brought his uncle’s drum. The coal cart was paid sixpence to drive past, and did nothing. Everything was too sharp, or too near. A barge is a long slow weight, and what it sends through the ground is more like a held note than a knock.

Ilse thanked everybody and gave the apprentices a sheet of marbled paper each. Then she sat down on the step. She was not exactly beaten, but she was out of ideas.

volumes.title: The Ten Past Four
volumes.text:
Ilse Farrow had stopped trying. That is the only reason she was at her trough in the Ropewalk wash-house at ten past four, combing an ordinary sheet. She had her grandmother’s colours and the brown river water, and had given up on the shiver that made every line of the old paper run double.

Emberwick has a branch railway, and its afternoon goods train crosses the iron bridge over the Ember, slowly, with coal. Ilse had heard it every day since April and never listened.

The comb was halfway down the trough when a hum came up through the floor. The surface shivered. Every line stood for an instant beside its own twin. She dropped the comb and laid the paper down with both hands. When she lifted it, the veins ran double from edge to edge. She held it by the corners, dripping, long after the train had gone.

volumes.title: Written Down This Time
volumes.text:
There are two goods trains a day over the Ember bridge, so through that winter Ilse Farrow made two sheets a day of the shivered paper. She stood in the wash-house on Ropewalk with the sheet in her hands, listening, as her grandmother Marta once stood listening for barges.

Marta had given her pattern no name, and told nobody how it was done, and it had cost her granddaughter nine years. Ilse called hers the Ten Past Four. She had the binder in Needle Lane make a plain book with the first matched pair as endpapers, and on its first page she wrote the whole method: river water in autumn, earth from the Fells, and wait for something heavy going by.

Then she put it in the hatbox beside her grandmother’s, paid a second year’s rent, and saw at last to the drain the dyer next door had complained of.

volumes.title: Left on the Step
volumes.text:
Repair ledger of Dorcas Venn, book mender, Bridge Street, Emberwick. Sign over the door: No Book Refused. First frost of November.

Book: An Alphabet of Animals. Brought by: nobody. It was on the step when I opened, wrapped in a flour sack. Complaint: spine gone, sewing perished, every corner soft as cloth. Wants the letter Q. Pinned inside, a note in thick flat pencil: Please mend. Will pay when I come. Do not throw away the loose bits.

No name. In nineteen years every book has come attached to a person, who told me rather more than I asked. This one came with only a sack. Someone has read it nearly to pieces; the page for B, a badger, is worn pale by a thumb far larger than a child’s. Treatment: resewn, new cloth spine, loose bits kept. Shelved under Unclaimed, where it is the only book.

volumes.title: Stuck at Puddings
volumes.text:
From the repair ledger of Dorcas Venn, book mender, Bridge Street, Emberwick. December. Book: a household receipt book, handwritten, three generations of ink. Brought by: young Wilf Pargeter, for his grandmother, who made him swear an oath first. Complaint: will not open at Puddings.

Cause: treacle, of some age. Eleven pages had become one. I parted them over the steam of the kettle, a leaf an hour, across two days. Under the treacle lay the Midwinter pudding the whole Pargeter family has argued about since the old lady’s mother died. It wants a spoonful of strong tea. Nobody had guessed tea.

Mrs Pargeter’s orders, by way of Wilf: mend it but do not clean it; the gravy on page nine was her wedding day. So the stains stay. Paid in pudding. The alphabet book left nameless on my step last month is still on the Unclaimed shelf. I dust it.

volumes.title: The Verger’s Mouse
volumes.text:
Ledger of Dorcas Venn, mender of books, Bridge Street, Emberwick. January, bitter. Book: the bell-ringers’ book from the church tower. Brought by: Mr Crake, verger, holding it at arm’s length. Complaint: mice.

One mouse, and a tidy one. She had eaten the index and the lower margin of forty pages, taking care to leave the print, and built from the crumbs a nest in the hollow of the spine. The ringers’ changes are all there. Only the white is gone. I told Mr Crake his mouse could evidently read. He did not smile.

Treatment: new margins grafted on in matched paper, new spine. The nest I returned to Mr Crake in a matchbox, it being church property. Still on my Unclaimed shelf: one child’s alphabet, left on the step in November with no name. No mouse would have got at that book. Somebody held it too often.

volumes.title: Where the Thumb Rests
volumes.text:
Repair ledger of Dorcas Venn, book mender, Bridge Street, Emberwick. February. Book: a sea atlas of the Grey Coast, salt-stiff, forty charts. Brought by: Captain Ives Tarrant, retired, who stood while I looked. Complaint: one chart, the ninth, has split along its fold.

It had not split. It had been worn through. Chart nine shows Saltby and the bar, and there is a hole in the paper just off the harbour mouth, the size and shape of a thumb. He has been coming home on that page for thirty years, with his finger always on the one place.

Treatment: chart lined with thin linen; hole filled with toned paper. I asked whether I should ink the lost soundings back in. He said no, he knew the depth there. The alphabet book somebody left unnamed on my step in November has a thumb-worn page too. I notice thumbs now.

volumes.title: Twelve Broken Grammars
volumes.text:
From the ledger of Dorcas Venn, book mender, Bridge Street, Emberwick. March. Books: twelve copies of the same school grammar. Brought by: Mr Phineas Lark, schoolmaster, in a wheelbarrow. Complaint: all broken, all at once.

All broken, I found, at the same place. Every one fell open at page forty and went no further. Page forty is the irregular verbs. I laid them in a row for Mr Lark and let him work it out. That is the page at which a child of nine puts the book down hard.

Treatment: twelve spines strengthened. I suggested, advice being free, that he might take page forty more slowly. He paid in full and said he would consider it. A thought, entered for want of anywhere else: the child’s alphabet left on my step in November broke nowhere in particular. It wore out evenly. Somebody went through it steadily, many times.

volumes.title: Jam, String, and Nell
volumes.text:
Repair ledger of Dorcas Venn, book mender, Bridge Street, Emberwick. April. Book: Mr Pudderby’s Snail, a picture book. Brought by: Nell Tibbet, aged seven, alone. Complaint: “I mended it and it got worse.”

She had. The loose pages were stuck in with plum jam and all tied round with garden string, bow on top. I have seen worse from grown binders. I took out the jam and kept the string as a bookmark. Paid: one bone button.

She stood on a box to watch, and spied the alphabet book on my Unclaimed shelf, left nameless on the step last November. She read it through and reported that there was no Q. I said I knew. She borrowed my pencil, drew a quail on a slip, more or less, and told me to put it in until the real one came. I have. It looks like a potato with opinions.

volumes.title: Too Full of Flowers
volumes.text:
From the ledger of Dorcas Venn, mender of books, Bridge Street, Emberwick. May. Book: a herbal, with coloured plates. Brought by: Miss Amabel Thrush of Marsh End. Complaint: will not shut.

Between every pair of pages lay a pressed flower: campion, marsh marigold, a whole flat foxglove. The spine had burst with the strain. I proposed removing them. Miss Thrush looked at me as if I had proposed removing her sister. Her sister Lettice pressed them, each at its own page, over forty summers, and now lies in the churchyard.

Treatment: resewn with a thin stub of paper bound in beside each leaf, to make room at the back for what is in the front. It shuts. Every flower is where Lettice put it. On the Unclaimed shelf, the alphabet left on my step last November waits. It holds no flowers, but I think it was loved as much.

volumes.title: Thirty Lambings
volumes.text:
Repair ledger of Dorcas Venn, book mender, Bridge Street, Emberwick. June. Book: a pocket notebook, black, swollen. Brought by: Old Garth, shepherd, down from the Northern Fells. Complaint: cover came off in the rain.

It has lived thirty years in one coat pocket. It records every lambing on Garth’s side of the fell: dates, weather, twins, and remarks on particular ewes that I shall not repeat. It smells of sheep. I reached for the sponge and he put his hand flat on the book. New cover. Nothing else. The smell, he said, was how he found it in the dark.

Treatment: new cover in oiled cloth. He checked my sum in pencil, thick and flat, the sort sharpened with a knife. I had seen that line before, on the note with the alphabet book left on my step last November. A working pencil, then, and a working hand.

volumes.title: The Missing Last Page
volumes.text:
From the ledger of Dorcas Venn, book mender, Bridge Street, Emberwick. July. Book: a novel, Miss Pellow of Gull Rock, from the lending shelves of the town library. Brought by: Miss Orla Finch, an assistant there. Complaint: last page missing, and has been for eleven years.

That has not stopped anyone borrowing it. Tucked inside the back cover I found twenty-three slips, each in a different hand, each supplying an ending. She marries the pilot. She sails away alone. In one, a whale is involved. Miss Finch had not the heart to throw any away.

Treatment: spine relined; all twenty-three slips bound in at the back, with ten blank leaves after them. I asked whether the library had missed a child’s alphabet; one has sat on my Unclaimed shelf since November. Nobody had asked, she said. She added that people who are learning do not always like to ask.

volumes.title: Two Halves, Two Sisters
volumes.text:
Repair ledger of Dorcas Venn, book mender, Bridge Street, Emberwick. September. Book: a family birthday book. Brought by: Mrs Hobday, on Tuesday, who had January to June. And by Mrs Peverel, on Thursday, who had July to December. Complaint, from each: the other half is missing.

They are sisters. The book came apart during a disagreement forty years ago, and each went home with what she was holding. Neither knew the other had been in. I did not say.

Treatment: resewn as one book, the bill divided in two. I told each it would be ready on Saturday at three. They arrived together, and it was quiet in my shop for a while. Then Mrs Hobday found a birthday entered wrong. My Unclaimed shelf still holds a child’s alphabet left on the step ten months ago. Not every owner comes back within the week, or the decade.

volumes.title: The Sack Is Recognised
volumes.text:
From the ledger of Dorcas Venn, mender of books, Bridge Street, Emberwick. October. Book: the day book of Hallow Mill in the Lowlands. Brought by: Jem Rudge, its carter. Complaint: floury, and the hinges gone.

While I looked it over, he looked over my shop, and stopped at the Unclaimed shelf. Beside the child’s alphabet I keep the flour sack it arrived in, eleven months ago, on my step. “That is one of ours,” said Jem. So it was; the mill’s mark was on the seam, and I had never thought to look.

Most Hallow Mill flour goes down the Ember by barge, and the bargeman is Abel Strand, a quiet man who writes his tallies with a carpenter’s pencil. Abel went downriver last November. His barge was sold at Saltby, and he has been working the coast to buy another. Treatment: hinges renewed. Jem will pass the word.

volumes.title: Q Comes Home
volumes.text:
Repair ledger of Dorcas Venn, Bridge Street, Emberwick. First frost of November, a year on. Book: An Alphabet of Animals, left on my step in a flour sack. Called for by: Abel Strand, bargeman, who filled the doorway and took off his hat.

The book was his daughter Minnie’s. When she was grown she taught him his letters from it, as far as P. Then she married, and he went on alone and stuck at Q. Out of his hatband he took a folded page: Q, a quail. He had carried it all year to practise on. The rest he got from the names painted on boats.

I gave him his bill. He read it aloud, slowly: Alphabet, resewn, new spine, one shilling. Treatment: Q mended in beside the quail a child drew to keep its place. He wanted both. The Unclaimed shelf is empty but for the sack, folded.
